routes.description: Establish that God is required to ground objective moral value and duty and to provide the ultimate significance and accountability that complete an objective moral framework.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if intrinsic value is grounded in God's nature, categorical duty in divine commands rather than convention, and the lasting significance and accountability of moral action in a theistic order.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective values, duties, human significance, and accountability jointly require God.

centralBridges.description: Ground intrinsic human worth and objective goodness in God's nature while explaining why naturalistic capacities or evolutionary origins are insufficient.
Ground categorical moral obligations in divine commands and distinguish genuine duties from social conditioning, agreement, or convention.
Explain why enduring moral significance and ultimate accountability require consequences beyond extinction and temporal human affairs.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how divine accountability reconciles moral obligation with prudential reasons and supports responsible moral agency.
Distinguish fallible moral knowledge from objective truth and preserve transcultural criticism of conduct and institutions.

routes.description: Establish that stance-independent moral reasons, objective duties, human significance, and responsibility can be explained within secular moral realism without a divine ground or eternal consequences.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if secular accounts supply objective moral standards and categorical reasons, explain responsible agency and moral criticism, and show that finite harms, benefits, relationships, and actions retain real significance without cosmic permanence.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular moral realism can adequately ground every objective moral domain placed in dispute without requiring God.

centralBridges.description: Explain objective morality through desire-independent categorical reasons, substantive harm-and-help standards, or basic moral facts.
Explain moral requirements through decisive reasons or fair rational agreement without presupposing a personal lawgiver.
Ground genuine human significance in the objective importance of finite lives, harms, relationships, and actions rather than eternal cosmic effects.
Ground responsibility in rational agency and defend the authority of moral reasons even when morality conflicts with prudential self-interest.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain disagreement and historical moral error as compatible with objective truth and corrigible through reflective reasoning.
Demonstrate how secular principles yield determinate judgments about atrocities, innocent victims, and harms to sentient animals.

sections.title: Objective Value and Intrinsic Human Worth
sections.rationale: The motion requires an account of what makes value stance-independent and whether human worth is grounded by God, rational capacities, harm, or irreducible moral facts.

sections.title: Moral Duty, Categorical Reasons, and Lawgiving
sections.rationale: The principal grounding clash concerns whether genuine obligation needs divine command or can arise from objective reasons, rational agreement, and mutual moral authority.

sections.title: Rational Agency and Naturalistic Grounding
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether reflective capacities can explain moral responsibility and wrongness, or merely identify valuable features whose objective status still requires a deeper ground.

sections.title: Finite Life, Extinction, and Moral Significance
sections.rationale: The competing routes must establish whether actions and relationships need eternal consequences to matter objectively or possess genuine importance within finite human lives.

sections.title: Accountability, Salvation, and Prudential Conflict
sections.rationale: The accountability burden includes ultimate justice, the relation between morality and self-interest, and whether the proposed theistic mechanism consistently delivers deserved consequences.

sections.title: Moral Knowledge, Progress, and Practical Application
sections.rationale: Disagreement, historical error, atrocities, and treatment of animals test whether each foundation supports reliable moral criticism and substantive guidance without conflating access with truth.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Right and wrong can be grounded in whether conduct harms people or unjustifiably fails to help them.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan explicitly introduces this passage as his own illustrative outline of a plausible secular ethical theory.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies a substantive secular standard centered on harm and justified assistance, so no earlier opposing move requires an answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly advances a central bridge through a clear and practically usable substantive standard.

precisionFindings.rationale: The harm-and-help standard is recoverable, but the relevant circumstances and justification conditions remain only implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It is presented as a plausible outline rather than a complete theory, matching the illustrative support actually supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Harm and failure to help coherently organize familiar rules, though the bridge from harm to objective wrongness remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete moral considerations support the outline, but no developed defense resolves conflicts, thresholds, or rival explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies substantive content for the indispensable secular objective-reasons bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move proposes its own illustrative standard and does not materially characterize a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly identifies hurting people and relevant failures to help as the basis of wrong action and ordinary moral rules.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Objective moral facts consist in overriding categorical reasons that do not depend on anyone's opinions, desires, or goals.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage continues Kagan's uninterrupted opening case and repeatedly states his account in explicit first-person terms.

response.rationale: This constructive move defines objectivity through universal, overriding categorical reasons independent of individual desires or goals, without answering an earlier opponent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the central secular-realist thesis explicitly and connects objectivity to desire-independent reasons.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition and its categorical, desire-independent scope are explicit and consistently stated in the supplied passage.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The definition is asserted confidently, while the deeper defense of categorical authority is largely assumed rather than demonstrated here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The account clearly connects objective wrongness with universal overriding reasons, but their source and authority remain an implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The rape example illustrates the claim, but the move offers limited independent warrant that such categorical reasons exist.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This is a direct and explicit statement of the secular route's central objective-reasons requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage develops a positive account and does not depend on interpreting or weakening an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says everyone has overriding categorical reasons regardless of their particular desires or goals and applies this to rape.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Objective moral rules can be grounded in those that perfectly rational agents would agree to behind a veil of ignorance.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan introduces contractarianism by name and develops its bargaining procedure, objectivity, and necessity in one sustained passage.

response.rationale: This constructive move offers ideal rational agreement behind a veil of ignorance as a secular account of the origin and objectivity of moral rules.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies a recognizable duty-generating procedure, though several constraints on agreement remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contract procedure is recoverable, but what perfect rationality requires and which bargaining constraints apply remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account is offered as a candidate deeper story and question about objectivity, appropriately short of claiming a completed derivation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The procedure can coherently generate impartial rules, but the inference from hypothetical agreement to categorical duty needs a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The veil-of-ignorance device is explained, but its authority and unique outcomes are not defended against competing contract specifications.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central secular-duty bridge by proposing an impartial rational basis for requirements.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily constructs a secular contractual account rather than assessing a developed opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grounds governing rules in what agents would give themselves while perfectly rational and ignorant of their identities.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Moral requirements need no personal lawgiver, just as the requirement of non-contradiction needs no cosmic logician.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan states the lawgiver objection, tests it through an extended analogy, and explicitly gives his skeptical conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move attacks the claimed need for a personal lawgiver through an analogy with the impersonal law of non-contradiction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it explicitly contests an indispensable divine-lawgiver premise with a clear counterexample structure.

precisionFindings.rationale: The analogy and its limited conclusion—that genuine requirements need not be personally enacted—are plainly recoverable and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues that personified language does not entail a person and draws a proportionate analogous conclusion about morality.

charity.alternative: Moral obligations differ from logical requirements because obligations characteristically involve authoritative commands.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy rebuts a general lawgiver requirement but does not fully establish that moral and logical normativity are equivalent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy validly challenges the universal lawgiver premise, though it does not by itself supply a complete theory of moral authority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The logical comparison is specific and relevant, but the move only briefly addresses whether moral obligation is importantly disanalogous.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable pro central bridge claiming that objective duty requires divine commands.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly isolates the lawgiver inference, although it leaves the strongest disanalogy between logical and moral requirements underdeveloped.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies that non-contradiction requires a personal legislator and expressly extends that point to genuine moral requirements.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: God's holy and loving nature supplies an objective standard of value, while naturalism leaves human worth dependent on contingent evolutionary adaptations.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this his first claim and develops it continuously through divine-nature grounding and a naturalistic evolutionary contrast.

components.text: Explain what supplies the objective standard and intrinsic worth behind categorical moral reasons.
Explain why human beings and their harms possess objective rather than merely contingent value.

response.rationale: The move contacts both secular value proposals by offering God's nature as the standard and challenging whether contingent evolution can ground human worth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive grounding demand, but largely asserts the divine solution and does not closely test the secular basic-fact account.

precisionFindings.rationale: Divine nature is clearly identified as the standard, but the move shifts between grounding goodness generally and grounding human worth.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The excerpt supports a theistic grounding proposal but does not establish the stronger claim that no secular basis for worth remains.

charity.alternative: Secular realism may treat persons, harms, or categorical reasons as basic objective facts rather than evolutionary preferences.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evolutionary explanation of belief does not alone show that the believed value is subjective or false.

logicalCoherence.rationale: God's nature can function as a proposed standard, but the necessity inference relies on an unsupported evolutionary-or-objective dichotomy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Divine attributes and evolutionary contingency are asserted, with limited warrant that the former grounds value or exhausts secular alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro bridge concerning objective value and intrinsic human worth.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the secular claim but compresses it into contingent evolutionary adaptation without answering its realist formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls God's holy and loving nature the absolute standard, then asks what basis for human moral worth remains without God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral duties require commands flowing from God's moral nature because social conditioning and social contracts yield conventions rather than genuine obligations.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly marks this as his second argument and contrasts divine commands with the secular social-contract account attributed to Kagan.

components.text: Show why ideal rational agreement produces genuine obligation rather than convention.
Determine whether objective moral requirements need a personal source of authoritative commands.

response.rationale: The move directly contrasts divine commands with social contract and convention, contacting the authority question raised by both earlier secular moves.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It reaches the decisive authority issue, but does not answer the non-contradiction analogy or the idealized character of Kagan's contract.

precisionFindings.rationale: The command-based account and convention contrast are clear, though the exclusivity of the proposed source is only implicitly defended.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The passage explains how commands could ground duties but does not establish that every secular account reduces to social conditioning or convention.

charity.alternative: Ideal rational agreement purports to identify objective rules rather than report an actual society's conventions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling the proposal a social contract does not show that its ideal rational constraints are conventional.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The positive command account is intelligible, but the inference from objective obligation to a commander remains substantially unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Traditional commandments and necessary divine nature are invoked, while rival impersonal and contractual accounts receive little comparative defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the indispensable pro central bridge grounding objective duties in divine commands.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply targets contractarianism but materially weakens it by treating ideal rational agreement as ordinary social convention.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines objective duties, locates them in divine commandments, and says those commands necessarily flow from God's moral nature.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Moral responsibility applies to rational agents because they can reflect on reasons and regulate their behavior, unlike animals or very young children.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator-free exchange clearly shifts from Craig's challenge to Kagan's extended first-person answer and examples.

components.text: Explain the morally relevant distinction between reflective persons and nonreflective animals under naturalism.

response.rationale: The move answers the naturalistic differentiation challenge by identifying reflection on reasons and behavioral regulation as the relevant capacity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly supplies the requested naturalistic distinction, though it explains responsibility more fully than intrinsic objective worth.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between reflective agents and nonreflective creatures is clearly specified and consistently tied to responsibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The straightforward agency distinction is supported by the lion comparison without claiming that it completes every grounding question.

charity.alternative: The challenge concerns why reflective capacities are objectively valuable, not merely which beings can deliberate.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reflective control explains responsibility but does not alone establish the objective value of the capacity or its possessor.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Reflective recognition and behavioral control coherently distinguish responsible agents, with one bounded bridge from reasons-responsiveness to responsibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The lion-human contrast is concrete and apt, though broader conditions for responsibility and impaired agency are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central secular responsibility bridge by grounding responsibility in rational reflective agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer fairly addresses the agency aspect of the challenge, while leaving the deeper value-grounding qualification unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts lions unable to reflect with humans who can recognize reasons and regulate conduct accordingly.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Once agents can step back from conduct, assess standards, and recognize reasons against harm, no additional supernatural ingredient is required for wrongness.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan explicitly restates Craig's revised question and answers it continuously in the first person throughout the window.

components.text: Answer why naturalistic reflective capacities are insufficient without a supernatural ground.
Explain how reasons and standards can guide conduct without an additional divine command.

response.rationale: The reply claims that reflective assessment and recognition of reasons put the required moral machinery in place, directly denying a further supernatural ingredient.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly rejects the need for an added ingredient, but the objective authority of the recognized standards remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The sufficiency claim is clear, but endorsed standards and independently valid reasons are not sharply distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Reflective capacity supports moral agency, but the claim that all necessary machinery is thereby present outruns the stated grounding argument.

charity.alternative: The theistic challenge grants reflective capacities but asks what makes their standards and objects objectively valuable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Capacity to assess reasons does not by itself establish that the reasons assessed are objectively authoritative.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The agency account is coherent, but sufficiency depends on an unargued bridge from reflective endorsement to objective moral reasons.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evolutionary-reflective mechanism is described, while its connection to stance-independent normativity remains materially compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro central value bridge by denying that naturalistic capacities need further supernatural grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses supernatural supplementation but partly substitutes an agency explanation for the opponent's deeper value-grounding demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says evolved creatures capable of stepping back, assessing standards, and recognizing reasons possess the needed moral machinery.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Identifying distinctive human capacities such as reflection, love, creativity, and communication does not yet explain why those capacities or their possessors are objectively valuable under naturalism.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig refers to Kagan's book and frames the passage as his own challenge concerning explanatory grounding under naturalism.

components.text: Show that identifying reflective capacities explains why those capacities and persons are objectively valuable.
Distinguish an explanation of responsible agency from an explanation of objective worth.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the missing explanatory step: naming distinctive capacities or intrinsic value does not ground their objective goodness under naturalism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the omitted inference and states why the naturalistic capacity account does not complete the value-grounding demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between identifying valuable capacities and explaining their objective value is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move raises a targeted explanatory challenge rather than claiming that no secular answer could possibly be supplied.

charity.alternative: A secular realist may regard persons or their capacities as irreducibly and intrinsically valuable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Basic-value stopping points are possible, although the opponent may legitimately ask whether they are adequately explanatory.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between locating value-bearing features and grounding their value is clear and exposes a genuine explanatory gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The quoted intrinsic-value stopping point supports the diagnosis, though no independent argument proves that all basic secular facts are illegitimate.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central secular objective-reasons bridge at its grounding step.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately recognizes the intrinsic-value response and challenges its explanatory stopping point without converting it into subjectivism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grants the claimed goods but asks whether simply regarding persons as intrinsically valuable cuts off explanation too soon.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: If naturalism ends in universal extinction with no ultimate accountability, moral choices lack enduring significance because every outcome leaves the final universe neither better nor worse.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig answers Kagan's direct question and develops his familiar heat-death and accountability argument in a continuous response.

components.text: Show why categorical moral reasons cease to matter merely because all life eventually ends.
Explain why present harms and benefits lack significance unless they alter the universe's final state.

response.rationale: The extinction scenario bears on significance but does not answer the secular claim that finite harms and categorical reasons can be objectively important now.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It offers relevant contrary material, yet leaves the decisive inference from eventual extinction to present insignificance unsupported.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move slides between enduring cosmic effect, accountability, and significance without specifying why only permanence constitutes significance.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker marks difficulty understanding significance, but the implied conclusion remains much stronger than the extinction premise warrants.

charity.alternative: Finite events may possess objective importance for affected beings even if their effects are not eternal.
charity.decisiveQualification: Lack of permanent cosmic difference does not entail lack of temporally located or relational objective value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core inference from eventual extinction to no moral significance is a substantial non sequitur absent a permanence requirement.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The physical extinction scenario is described, but no warrant establishes that only final cosmic states determine moral importance.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro significance-and-accountability bridge despite the weak inferential connection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move focuses on eternal outcome and largely omits the strongest finite-significance interpretation of the secular position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes a future of dead stars and no accountability, then infers that choices leave the universe neither better nor worse.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Torture matters objectively to victims, families, and communities even if it never changes the universe's eternal endpoint.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan directly challenges Craig's heat-death response, using Craig's torture example and repeatedly distinguishing local importance from cosmic permanence.

components.text: Show why torture lacks significance unless it changes the universe's eternal endpoint.

response.rationale: The reply directly identifies the extinction inference as mistaken and states the defeating consequence: torture matters to victims and communities without cosmic permanence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the decisive inference and supplies a concrete counterexample to the claimed permanence condition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited claim that finite torture can matter objectively without cosmic effect is clear, stable, and fully explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The concrete claim that torture matters to its victims is proportionate and directly defeats the universal insignificance inference.

charity.alternative: The pro argument may concern ultimate or enduring significance rather than every form of local importance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even that distinction cannot support the broader claim that finite moral choices have no objective significance at all.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The victim-centered counterexample validly shows that no eternal cosmic difference is required for at least some objective significance.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Torture supplies a specific and compelling counterexample, though a complete metaphysics of finite value is not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central secular finite-significance bridge and attacks the rival permanence condition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly isolates the permanence premise while preserving the distinction between cosmic endurance and genuine finite importance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says torture matters to victims and denies that this requires an eternal difference to the universe.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: On atheism prudential self-interest can conflict with moral duty, whereas divine accountability ultimately reconciles prudent action with morally required sacrifice.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly clarifies his third argument, contrasts atheism with theism, and confirms Kagan's summary of his proposed reconciliation.

components.text: Explain why prudential self-interest defeats rather than merely conflicts with overriding categorical moral reasons.
Show why finite harms lose moral authority when wrongdoing can serve the agent's interests.

response.rationale: The move introduces divine reconciliation of prudence and morality but does not answer the secular claim that moral reasons can rationally override self-interest.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant to practical authority, yet leaves the decisive claim that prudence must trump morality largely asserted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alleged conflict is clear, but prudence, rational authority, and self-interest are treated as interchangeable without qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that prudence trumps morality on naturalism is stronger than the mere possibility of conflict established in the passage.

charity.alternative: Objective moral reasons may rationally outweigh prudential reasons even when compliance harms the agent.
charity.decisiveQualification: Conflict with self-interest does not establish either irrationality or the absence of objective obligation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Divine consequences could align incentives, but the inference that naturalistic prudence necessarily defeats morality is substantially unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Possible conflicts are familiar and concrete, yet no comparative warrant establishes prudence's overriding authority or theism's truth.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary pro bridge concerning prudence, accountability, and agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move notices conflict but largely assumes the disputed priority of prudence instead of engaging the strongest secular account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt claims prudential and moral value conflict under naturalism and contrasts this with ultimate accountability under theism.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Conflict between morality and prudence does not establish that self-interest prevails, because moral reasons may carry greater rational weight.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan rejects Craig's characterization of his view and then formulates a direct question about why moral reasons cannot outweigh prudential ones.

components.text: Show that conflict between morality and self-interest entails that prudence rationally overrides morality.

response.rationale: The reply expressly denies the missing inference: acknowledging conflict does not imply that self-interest supplies the only or strongest rational reasons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It identifies the decisive unsupported priority claim and preserves the legitimate point that the two kinds of reason may conflict.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between conflict and rational priority is explicit, stable, and confined to the relevant inference.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical point that conflict alone does not establish prudential priority is fully supported by the exchange.

charity.alternative: The theistic argument may claim that unresolved conflict makes morality practically irrational, not merely inconvenient.
charity.decisiveQualification: That stronger claim still requires an argument that prudential reasons necessarily dominate categorical moral reasons.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response correctly distinguishes the existence of conflicting reasons from any conclusion about which reasons rationally prevail.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is decisive for the stated inference, though the positive ranking of moral reasons is only briefly developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central secular responsibility bridge concerning morality's authority against prudential self-interest.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately reconstructs the intended conflict while exposing the exact additional premise needed for the conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts that morality and self-interest may conflict while denying that this makes self-interest the only rational consideration.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Fair rational agreement condemns Nazi killing objectively because perfectly rational bargainers behind appropriate constraints would prohibit killing innocent people.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan gives an uninterrupted answer to an audience question about whether victorious Nazis could determine morality by controlling society.

components.text: Demonstrate that secular contractual rules can yield objective condemnation rather than mere social convention.
Show that rationally constrained agreement prohibits serious wrongdoing despite an offender's interests.

response.rationale: The move applies ideal contractarian constraints to Nazi killing and derives a prohibition on killing innocent people, contacting the practical objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It reaches the decisive application demand, but acknowledges that the derivation of the contractual prohibition is not supplied in detail.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim, ideal-bargainer scope, and prohibition on killing innocent people are explicit and consistently distinguished from actual Nazi opinion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges that the argument needs more time, but still asserts an outcome whose derivation remains compressed.

charity.alternative: A divine-command critic may argue that hypothetical agreement still lacks categorical authority even when it condemns atrocities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Correct practical output demonstrates determinacy but does not by itself establish the procedure's ultimate authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Ideal bargaining can coherently prohibit victimizing innocents, but the specific derivation and authority bridge remain materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Nazi case is concrete, yet the speaker expressly postpones the argument showing why every ideal bargain adopts this prohibition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary practical-application bridge with a determinate secular judgment about atrocity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly addresses the convention objection at the application level while leaving the deeper authority challenge intact.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes actual Nazi approval from ideal rational agreement and states that the latter prohibits killing innocent people.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Recognizing religious atrocities as wrong supports objective moral criticism, while such criticism requires a transcendent standard rather than the mere fact that a person believes in God.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig answers an audience question in the first person, gives several religious examples, and explicitly distinguishes moral belief from moral grounding.

components.text: Show why ideal rational condemnation of Nazi killing requires a transcendent divine standard.
Answer the claim that genuine objective requirements need no personal lawgiver.

response.rationale: The reply clarifies that belief in God is unnecessary for moral conduct, but it asserts rather than establishes that objective criticism needs God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The material is issue-bearing and clarificatory, yet it does not contact the secular contract's claimed objective authority or its derivation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between believing in God and God serving as an ontological standard is clearly and explicitly maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Examples of recognized wrongdoing support objectivity but do not establish the stronger necessity of a divine transcendent standard.

charity.alternative: Secular categorical reasons or ideal rational agreement may permit criticism beyond a society's actual beliefs.
charity.decisiveQualification: Transcending actual opinion does not entail dependence on a divine person or nature.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The belief-versus-ontology distinction is coherent, but the inference from objective criticism to a specifically divine standard is unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Atrocity examples establish shared critical judgments, not the exclusive metaphysical explanation claimed for those judgments.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary pro bridge concerning transcultural criticism and fallible moral belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move rejects crude subjectivism but does not engage the strongest secular account already offered for transcultural criticism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes needing belief in God for morality from needing God as an objective transcendent standard beyond social belief.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Christian salvation through Christ appears to conflict with moral accountability because an evildoer may escape deserved punishment through repentance.
moves.attributionBasis: The question explicitly contrasts salvation through Jesus with Craig's preceding account of accountability and is followed by Craig's direct answer.

components.text: Explain how ultimate accountability remains consistent when repentant evildoers may avoid personally bearing punishment.
Clarify whether the proposed theistic system consistently holds serious wrongdoers accountable.

response.rationale: The move identifies an internal tension between deserved punishment and salvation through repentance, directly contacting the accountability mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely raises the decisive consistency problem, although it is framed as a question and does not yet defeat possible substitutionary answers.

precisionFindings.rationale: The apparent tension among punishment, repentance, salvation, and accountability is clearly stated as a challenge rather than a conclusion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker says the views appear to be in tension and requests reconciliation, exactly matching the limited support available.

charity.alternative: Christian accountability may permit forgiveness while maintaining that justice is satisfied through another mechanism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Unless that mechanism is supplied, an evildoer's escape from personally deserved punishment remains an apparent tension.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given the stated conception of accountability as deserved punishment, salvation of an evildoer generates a clear prima facie tension.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The tension follows from the described doctrines, though their precise theological formulation and possible reconciliation are not yet examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central pro significance-and-accountability bridge by testing the consistency of ultimate justice.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge is cautiously framed and leaves room for a doctrinal reconciliation rather than assuming that none exists.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how punishment of evildoers can be reconciled with salvation through Christ after repentance.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Christian salvation preserves divine justice because Christ bears the deserved penalty for sin, allowing repentant sinners to receive grace without eliminating accountability.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig expressly introduces the Christian view and gives a continuous theological answer to Kagan's immediately preceding salvation challenge.

components.text: Explain how salvation can forgive repentant sinners without leaving the deserved penalty unpaid.

response.rationale: The reply answers the stated tension by claiming that Christ bears the penalty demanded by divine justice, preserving punishment while permitting grace.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supplies the missing reconciliation mechanism, although it does not defend the justice of transferring punishment to another person.

precisionFindings.rationale: The substitutionary mechanism, the deserved penalty, and the beneficiary's receipt of grace are clearly and consistently specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The mechanism answers internal consistency, but its claim to preserve justice assumes rather than defends the legitimacy of substitution.

charity.alternative: Accountability may require the wrongdoer personally to bear deserved consequences rather than transferring them to an innocent substitute.
charity.decisiveQualification: Substitution preserves payment of a penalty only if vicarious punishment itself is just and relevantly attributable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Substitution provides an internally intelligible reconciliation, but the move leaves a material bridge about transferred punishment and personal desert.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Christian doctrine is clearly stated, yet no independent warrant is supplied for the justice or efficacy of penal substitution.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro significance-and-accountability bridge by addressing the salvation objection to justice.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply answers nonpayment but omits the strongest qualification concerning personal responsibility and the justice of substitution.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says Christ bears the deserved penalty under divine justice so sinners may receive grace without the penalty going unpaid.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Cultural disagreement reflects fallible and selfish human access to moral truth rather than the absence of objective values, and a transcendent standard permits criticism of corrupt societies.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig distinguishes moral epistemology from ontology in his characteristic framework and then invokes a transcendent standard against sociocultural relativism.

response.rationale: This constructive move distinguishes moral ontology from fallible moral knowledge and explains disagreement through selfishness and imperfect access to truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly protects objective truth from an epistemic disagreement objection and supports transcultural criticism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ontology-access distinction and the fallibility qualification are explicit, stable, and carefully confined to moral knowledge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers fallibility and selfishness as compatible explanations, without claiming that every disagreement has that source.

charity.alternative: Persistent disagreement may be evidence against reliable access to objective moral truth even if it does not logically disprove truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: Separating truth from access answers entailment but does not by itself establish reliable moral knowledge or explain every pattern of disagreement.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction correctly blocks a direct inference from disagreement or error to the nonexistence of objective moral facts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Human selfishness and fallibility are plausible explanations, though the move offers limited evidence about their adequacy across cultures.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary pro bridge concerning disagreement, moral access, and transcultural criticism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately addresses the ontological inference while leaving the strongest epistemic evidential concern available.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly separates moral ontology from knowledge and attributes failures to grasp truth partly to human selfishness and fallibility.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Secular moral realism can explain widespread historical error as gradual discovery through reasoning that corrects inherited tendencies.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan explicitly agrees with much of Craig's diagnosis, then supplies an evolutionary and rational account of progress toward recognition of moral truths.

components.text: Explain how secular agents can correct widespread inherited moral error through reflective reasoning.

response.rationale: The reply agrees that error need not eliminate truth and adds a secular discovery model in which civilization gradually recognizes moral facts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the epistemic-progress component directly, though the mechanism and reliability of reflection are only sketched by analogy.

precisionFindings.rationale: Gradual moral discovery is clear, but the scope of progress and the standards distinguishing discovery from change remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents gradual recognition as a partial explanation and appropriately avoids claiming uniform or inevitable progress.

charity.alternative: Historical change may reflect altered preferences or power rather than discovery of objective truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: A progress account needs independent standards for identifying correction rather than merely later consensus.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Gradual discovery coherently reconciles error with realism, but the criterion for reliable correction remains an implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The analogy with discovery in other domains is relevant, though no representative history or reliability mechanism is developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary secular bridge concerning historical error, reflection, and moral progress.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly acknowledges appalling past codes but only briefly addresses how reflective change qualifies as genuine discovery.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explains appalling historical codes as delayed recognition of moral truth, analogous to gradual discovery in other domains.

moves.speaker: Shelly Kagan
moves.proposition: Finite loving relationships and moral actions can possess genuine objective value despite eventual death and cosmic extinction.
moves.attributionBasis: Kagan identifies the essential disagreement with Craig and develops a continuous closing argument using finite loving relationships as his central counterexample.

components.text: Show that lack of eternal cosmic significance entails lack of genuine objective significance.
Explain why finite loving and moral action cannot retain value without ultimate reward or punishment.

response.rationale: The reply explicitly diagnoses the equivocation between eternal cosmic impact and objective significance, then offers finite loving relationships as a counterexample.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It targets the decisive inference, states its failure, and supplies a concrete positive account of value that survives extinction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between eternal cosmic significance and genuine objective value is explicit and consistently applied to finite love.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The counterexample proportionately establishes that noneternal duration alone does not negate objective relational value.

charity.alternative: The theistic argument may reserve 'ultimate significance' for permanent cosmic consequences rather than deny all local value.
charity.decisiveQualification: That stipulation cannot establish the broader conclusion that finite actions lack genuine objective moral significance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response cleanly exposes the invalid inference and gives a coherent counterexample in objectively valuable finite relationships.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Loving relationships provide a concrete and representative case, though the underlying secular metaphysics remains only briefly stated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central secular finite-significance bridge and defeats the rival eternity requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the narrower concept of cosmic permanence while accurately rejecting its substitution for objective value generally.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes eternal cosmic significance from objective moral significance and identifies real loving relationships as genuinely valuable.
